criteria.description: Correctly identifies the force-closure metric with privileged pose/shape info as the teacher.
Correctly identifies the RGB-D-trained network as the student.

solutions.fullSolution: The teacher is the force-closure metric, computed offline with privileged exact shape/pose knowledge, generating grasp-quality labels for many candidates. The student is the trained network, seeing only realistic RGB-D input at training and deployment, learning to predict what the privileged computation would say without needing exact poses/shapes itself.

criteria.description: Correctly explains wasted capacity on non-viable points if not staged.
Correctly explains the benefit of tailored per-stage losses and cleaner training signal.

solutions.fullSolution: Most scene points aren't viable grasp locations; predicting detailed geometry for all of them regardless would waste capacity/signal. Staging separates viability (classification loss) from geometry (regression losses), each with its own tailored loss, and geometric capacity only ever trains on already-plausible points, a cleaner signal than mixing viable/non-viable points in one target.

criteria.description: Correctly contrasts MDP policies (sequential, reward-driven) with structured one-shot prediction.
Correctly explains that classical control executes the predicted target.

solutions.fullSolution: An MDP policy outputs low-level controls at every state, trained against reward accumulated over a trajectory. Grasp/flow-field prediction outputs a single structured target from one observation, no sequential decision-making or reward accumulation. That target is then executed by classical model-based control (operational-space control, IK), so the learning problem is one-shot structured prediction, not a sequential MDP.
